title: tiny circles as completion fuel
content:
my favorite process to generate creative momentum

tiny circles is a simple, conceptual practice that I find myself returning to in my day to day creative/business life, and teaching about in creative systems. this practice has been like a magic carpet that nimbly navigates me past overwhelm, stuckness, and all varieties of tentacles that inevitably come up in ambitious projects. I don’t normally do “tricks, tips, and tools,” but the simplicity and power of this is too useful not to write about.

here’s how it goes — this practice is simple, and infinitely repeatable.

at any point, in any project, when you feel it lagging (or before you even begin), take a moment to ask yourself:

what is the tiniest circle I can create here?


that is, what is the tiniest circle I can make — to create the most fractional feeling of completion, or sense of containment? a tiny circle is a tangible, concrete visualization of a single iteration, and follows all the rules of iterative creation (I write about this more in this post: make a version 0.1 to say hello, world).

overcoming starting inertia

convincing yourself that you’re creating a tiny circle — rather than hiking 1% of a long and arduous journey — helps overcome the feeling of being daunted by the vision, and paralyzed from movement. the idea is to keep you in continual, tiny motion — not linear, but circular.

making a closed container

why circle? a circle, unlike a line, is a closed loop. tiny cups can still hold water without leaking; tiny containers of something can still satiate you in a small way. the closed and contained nature of a thing makes it interactive, usable, therefore testable — in ways that a half formed thing, however grandiosely or elaborately imagined, will not.


finding circular momentum

completion creates momentum. the feeling of having created one circle gives you a sense of satisfaction, momentum, and relief. it eases (even if just a little bit) some sense of the built up pressure of unborn visions. it create a sense of centripetal force, which means you can keep moving around the circle, like a merry-go-round, or like on a carousel. the faster you go, the more it feels like you’ll be able to fly.


elasticity of expansion

when you have a tiny circle, stretching to make it bigger feels so much less hard and takes so much less energy expenditure than building a castle from scratch. you can take the foundation that exists, and add layers, floors, and rooms. I often have an inclination to burn things to the ground and start over, but the concept of moving in tiny circles make me feel grounded and supported — like I’m not hiking a long and difficult trail; I’m spinning in one place, like a ballerina, preparing for a moment of levitation. I will always have a starting point from which to begin.

applying this in day-to-day

I define what makes a “tiny circle” by thinking about what will make me feel even a tiny bit of completion. completion — rather than a sense of interruption — is something you feel in your body, when your energy has had time and space to flow in little cycle; however small. I ask:

what will help me feel a tiny bit of completion?
what will help my mind release this project or task, even just a little bit?
what will help me find circular momentum?

examples

  • when I write a new post on my journal, I always create the visual first. then I’ll write the fleshed out post, sometimes weeks later. the visual is my tiny circle.

  • when I started thinking about creative systems course, instead of working on the “landing page” immediately, I started with making a zine/microbook. it wasn’t exactly tiny — but it was a circle that created momentum for everything else to feel effortless.

  • when I build a website, I always start with imagining the website as 1 single page — then 3 pages — and I challenge myself to imagine the smallest, simplest possible iteration of it. it makes it crystal clear to me what’s absolutely, structurally essential, and what’s not. I call it a digital cocoon — a concept I teach about in house on the webs.

nonlinear growth

from this tiny circles concept, what excites me the most is to realize that it’s a model for navigating a nonlinear journey. we’re not trying to get from A to B — like running a marathon — but instead, we’re embracing that growth happens in circles, we’re deepening in the continual spiral. we’re learning how to construct these circles, and how to dance in them, and how to allow them to carry us inwards, deeper, and beyond.

and, if all else fails, I remind myself of this:

a tiny circle is infinitely better than nothing.
